hints: Think about what happens when bacteria in farm animals are exposed to the same antibiotic every day in their feed for a long time.
Remember how natural selection works in bacteria, and what that would mean if those bacteria later infect a human who needs the same antibiotic.
walkthrough:
**Spot the key situation**

Think like a biologist. Antibiotics in animal feed means huge numbers of bacteria get long, low-level exposure. That is perfect conditions for selection to happen.

Remember: antibiotics do not act on human cells, they act on bacteria.

**Apply natural selection for resistance**

In any bacterial population there is variation. A few cells may have a mutation that gives resistance. The antibiotic kills the sensitive ones and leaves the resistant ones to survive and reproduce. Soon the resistant allele becomes common.

**Link to human treatment**

If those resistant pathogenic bacteria spread to humans through food or contact, then using the same antibiotic to treat human disease will not work. That is why we keep animal-feed antibiotics separate from important human antibiotics.

options.A: Antibiotics target bacterial structures, not human cells, so human cells do not respond or stop responding to them.
options.B: Allergy is possible with any drug, but it is not the main evolutionary reason for keeping animal and human antibiotics separate.
options.C: Long-term use in animals selects for resistant pathogenic bacteria, so the same antibiotic would then fail when needed to treat humans.
options.D: Antibiotics can harm useful gut bacteria, but this side effect applies to all antibiotic use and does not explain why animal-feed types must be different.
